claims.text: Adding approximately 2–5 wt% silicon during boride-alloy synthesis, followed by homogenization, will produce uniform silicon segregation at grain boundaries.
Segregated silicon at boride grain boundaries will form localized silicide phases.
The resulting silicide phases will be stable under molten-aluminum exposure.
Grain-boundary silicide phases will act as diffusion barriers against aluminum ingress.
Silicon-induced interfacial chemical modification will decrease the thermodynamic driving force for reactions between molten aluminum and the boride matrix.
Silicon doping and homogenization will slow molten-aluminum corrosion kinetics relative to undoped boride components.
The silicon-doped and homogenized material will develop thinner reaction layers than the undoped baseline.
The silicon-doped and homogenized material will exhibit less weight loss than the undoped baseline.
The silicon-doped and homogenized material will maintain greater mechanical integrity after molten-aluminum exposure than the undoped baseline.
The corrosion-resistance improvement should remain effective during exposure to molten aluminum at 750–800°C.
Loss of uniform silicon segregation may reduce the effectiveness of the proposed corrosion barrier.
Variations in processing or local silicon concentration may alter barrier quality.
An inert synthesis atmosphere, optimized cooling rates, and post-synthesis homogenization are conditions associated with obtaining the intended silicon distribution.
Reaction-layer thickness can be evaluated by cross-sectional SEM and EDS.
The proposed comparison uses undoped boride components without the additional homogenization treatment as the baseline.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifically requires a homogenization heat treatment, whereas the intervention permits either homogenization or directional solidification; these processing routes are presented as alternatives without establishing that both produce the same mediator.
